beats.narration_text: Tree-based models see each quarter as an isolated snapshot — a flat row of features with no memory of what came before. An LSTM changes that. It unrolls across four to eight quarters per company, passing a hidden state forward through time. A gradual hedging ramp over four quarters is a different signal than a single-quarter spike, and the LSTM learns the difference from sequence structure alone. A lighter GRU variant trains thirty percent faster with comparable accuracy. Both now sit alongside the tree models — sequence-aware predictions complementing snapshot-based ones.

Not all analyst questions are equal. The system now profiles individual analysts — tracking their question types, difficulty levels, and how closely their framing aligns with management responses. This matters for dodge scoring. Dodging a hard question from a known tough analyst is less informative than dodging a routine question from a friendly one. The raw dodge score might be identical, but once you normalize for analyst difficulty, the signal diverges. The same evasion, weighted by who asked, tells a different story.

props.sparkLine: The same evasion, a different asker.

beats.narration_text: Twenty phases in, the system sees time through LSTM and GRU sequence models, reads the market environment through regime detection, understands who is asking the questions through analyst profiling, and can cite the actual transcripts when explaining its reasoning. Every layer of context — temporal, environmental, interpersonal — makes the signal more precise. The system doesn't just extract what was said. It remembers what was said before. Next week, we keep building.

Your turn. Most scoring systems treat every observation as independent, and most of them shouldn't. Paste this into Claude with a score you already produce and ask what it is currently blind to — the history behind each reading, the conditions it was taken under, and who or what generated it.
